source.title: A Generalist Intracortical Motor Decoder
source.authors: Joel Ye; F. Rizzoglio; Adam Smoulder; Hongwei Mao; Xuan Ma; Patrick J. Marino; Raeed Chowdhury; Dalton D. Moore; G. Blumenthal; William Hockeimer; Nicolas G. Kunigk; J. P. Mayo; A. Batista; S. Chase; Adam G. Rouse; Michael L. Boninger; Charles M. Greenspon; Andrew B. Schwartz; N. Hatsopoulos; Lee E. Miller; Kristofer E. Bouchard; J. Collinger; Leila Wehbe; R. Gaunt

record.tranche_reason: The study examines scaling and downstream performance in intracortical neural-data models, a different modality and training setting from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps and downstream decoding outcomes. It does not fit or assess the specified language-model held-out cross-entropy power laws, extrapolate from small runs to much larger runs, or identify a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Numerical curves shown only in figures are not transcribed in the supplied text; rows record the authors’ explicit textual summaries.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own scaling sweeps for intracortical neural-data Transformers: pretraining data from 1.5 hrs to 2 khrs and 45M vs 350M parameters. It reports how downstream decoding R2 changes with scale, which bears on V6 in a new modality. It fits no power laws. It measures no LM cross-entropy, extrapolation or compute-optimal split, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. Add that pretraining gains vanish beyond about 1.5 hrs of downstream data, so the authors judge NDT3's pretraining weak by CV/NLP standards. They attribute the limits to sensor variability (input-order sensitivity) and output stereotypy, not to the model architecture alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales an autoregressive Transformer on intracortical neural and behavioral data and evaluates decoding performance; it does not use the original language-model loss-fitting procedure or measure held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by downstream dataset and data scale; 2 khrs of pretraining helps only when paired with increased model size in the aggregate, and neural-only downstream decoding saturates after 25 hours. Fine-tuning and task setup also affect reported results.

fits_no_version.finding: Neural reconstruction loss improves with more pretraining data under both neural-only and joint objectives. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In intracortical neural-data Transformers, the self-supervised neural loss improves monotonically with pretraining data up to 200 hrs.

record.problems: The paper does not fit power laws or report numerical values for many scaling curves in the text. Aggregate evaluation covers 31 settings, but the authors note that the evaluation may be too small to distinguish some pretrained models statistically. Downstream benefits vary by task; some settings have high variability, and the authors describe H2 training and tuning as unstable.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed numerical or per-curve results visible only in Figs. 3, 9, 10, 11, 13, and 15 are not separately transcribed where the supplied text gives no corresponding numerical values. Other distribution-shift and architecture-ablation results were left out because they do not test the downstream scale-predictability version.

untested.parts: No language models and no held-out LM cross-entropy. No power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted law and no extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute sweep and no optimal parameter/token split. Only two model sizes.
Table 4 says shape was not systematically explored.
Neural-data modality, but no power-law form is fitted to upstream or downstream curves, so the 'same power-law form' is not tested.
No relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss is fitted. There is no language-model downstream task, and only a few scale points.
No fitted exponents or analysis of fitting choices.

missing.what: Upstream test-split pretraining R2: the 2 khr model degrades vs 200 hr at 45M and merely maintains it at 350M. Adding 200 hrs from other monkeys gives no gain over 1.5 hrs of task data. This is a non-monotone upstream scaling result relevant to V5 in the neural modality.
The pretraining benefit over from-scratch vanishes once downstream data exceeds about 1.5 hrs (0.5–5K points). Scaling benefits are confined to low downstream-data regimes.

Downstream probe through pretraining: the bimanual 25% gain is reached by epoch 20 and then plateaus while upstream metrics keep improving. Authors contrast this with correlated upstream–downstream progress in LMs.
25 hr and 70 hr models show downstream performance noisily related to data scale; the 25 hr model differs from the others.

record.verdict_notes: V6 is linked here on the reading that it is not restricted to language models; a strict LM-only reading would move all rows to fits_no_version. Only two model sizes and five or so data scales exist, and nothing is fitted, so 'predictably' cannot be assessed quantitatively. The 45M saturation at 2 khrs, relieved by 350M, is consistent with model size becoming the bottleneck, not a challenge to scaling as such. The study cites Kaplan et al. only for its FLOP formula.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model cross-entropy loss; no test of power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep to find a loss-minimising parameter/token split or its trend with compute.
Architecture shapes are not systematically explored to measure the effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices on loss.
The study uses neural data, but does not fit or test whether the same power-law form holds in this modality or under other training regimes.
Tests downstream motor-decoding performance against pretraining scale in intracortical neural models, not downstream language-model tasks or a relationship to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or analysis of fitting choices; variable scaling outcomes alone do not test the stated fit-dependence claim.

rows.subject: NDT3 models (aggregate across 31 evaluation settings)
rows.size_stated: 45M and 350M parameter models; pretraining data scales include 1.5 hours, 200 hours, and 2 khrs
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream decoding performance across pretraining-data and model-size scales.

conditions.value: 31 settings across downstream datasets and data scales

rows.baseline: From-scratch NDT3 and other pretrained NDT3 models
rows.value: From-scratch NDT3 outperformed the WF and NDT2 baselines; pretraining improved performance through 200 hours, and further scaling to 2 khrs helped only with 350M parameters. The 350M 2 khr model significantly outperformed other pretrained NDT3s except the 350M 200 hr model.
rows.uncertainty: FDR-corrected pairwise t-tests; the 350M 2 khr model was reported as significantly better than other pretrained NDT3s except the 350M 200 hr model. Evaluation averages 31 settings.
rows.locator: Section 3.1; Fig. 3D–E; Supplementary Section B.7 and Fig. 13
rows.note: The study reports aggregate performance across settings, not a fitted scaling law. It says other pretrained-model pairs were not significantly different.
rows.check: The value mixes in a comparison of the study's own method against baselines (from-scratch NDT3 vs WF/NDT2), which is not a scaling result. The scaling part is only partly positive. 2 khrs helps only with 350M. B.7 says the other pretrained pairs, except 25 hr, are statistically equivalent. Fig. 13A says performance is 'noisily related' to data scale. State should be partial, not observed.

source_check.correct: Aggregate downstream performance improves with pretraining through 200 hours. Scaling to 2000 hours helps only with increased model size to 350M. The 350M 2 khr model outperforms other pretrained NDT3s except 350M 200 hr in the main-text significance comparison. Remove the from-scratch NDT3 versus WF/NDT2 comparison from the scaling result.
source_check.problem: The value mixes a valid scaling result with an architecture/baseline comparison that does not test scaling.

rows.subject: NDT3 45M models
rows.operation_detail: Increased pretraining data scale and compared downstream decoding.
rows.value: Performance improved from 1.5 hours to 200 hours but saturated at 2 khrs.
rows.note: The authors describe an aggregate trend; they do not give numerical values in the text.

rows.subject: NDT3 models on the bimanual cursor-control task
rows.size_stated: 45M and 350M parameter models; pretraining scales include up to 2 khrs
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining-data scales and model sizes.
rows.baseline: Lower pretraining-data scales and from-scratch models
rows.value: Increasing pretraining data yielded gains at all downstream data scales; jointly scaling to 2 khrs and 350M parameters improved performance.
rows.uncertainty: Shading shows standard deviation on 3 tuning seeds in Fig. 3C.
rows.note: The authors contrast this task’s clear gains with the less clear self-paced reach result.

rows.subject: NDT3 models on the self-paced reach task
rows.size_stated: 45M and 350M parameter models; pretraining scales include up to 2 khrs
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining-data scales and model sizes.
rows.baseline: From-scratch NDT3 and lower pretraining-data scales
rows.value: The result was described as much less clear; the from-scratch NDT3 was competitive at all downstream data scales.
rows.uncertainty: Shading shows standard deviation on 3 tuning seeds in Fig. 3C.
rows.note: The text does not report a numerical effect size for this task.

rows.subject: NDT3 models on eight primary evaluation datasets
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining-data scales by task.
rows.baseline: From-scratch NDT3 and other pretrained NDT3 scales
rows.value: The authors report substantial variation by task: Critical Stability Task and Bimanual Task show the clearest scaling with pretraining data; FALCON tasks and Self-paced Reach are minimally affected; 2D + Click and Grasp show high variability, with strong degradation for the 350M 2 khr model at low downstream-data scales.
rows.uncertainty: Three model seeds are shown for fine-tuning in Fig. 11A; Grasp used 9 seeds instead of the standard 3.
rows.note: The paper attributes the low-data degradation of the 350M 2 khr model on Grasp to possible instability of full fine-tuning.

source_check.correct: Standard fine-tuning uses three seeds, but Grasp uses nine seeds because of high instability. Fig. 11's caption gives the general three-seed description.
source_check.locator_found: Section B.5, paragraph discussing 2D + Click and Grasp; Fig. 11 caption.
source_check.problem: The uncertainty description needs the nine-seed exception for Grasp.

rows.subject: NDT3 fine-tuned on FALCON H2 handwriting
rows.size_stated: 45M and 350M examples are shown in Fig. 10; exact sizes for the stated comparison are not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whether pretraining/fine-tuning improved sequence-to-sequence handwriting decoding.
rows.value: Fine-tuning appeared to degrade final solution quality and reduce the range of nontrivial hyperparameters.
rows.note: The authors state that they do not quantify the comparison to expected performance for unaugmented RNNs.
rows.check: This compares pretrained-then-fine-tuned vs from-scratch only, not a graded scale sweep. The degradation is described qualitatively ('appears'), without numbers. Reversed holds only in the sense that pretraining hurts.

source_check.correct: Fig. 10 identifies example runs as 45M 200h and Scratch; the text does not identify 350M handwriting examples. The authors qualitatively report worse final solution quality and a narrower range of nontrivial hyperparameters after fine-tuning.
source_check.locator_found: Section B.4; Fig. 10 legend and caption.
source_check.problem: The claim that 350M handwriting examples are shown is unsupported.

rows.subject: NDT3 neural-only-pretrained models fine-tuned on the Critical Stability Task
rows.stage_stated: neural-only pretrained, then fine-tuned with a newly initialized behavioral readout
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream decoding after neural-only pretraining at increasing data scales.
rows.value: Neural-only pretraining decoding performance saturated after 25 hours, unlike the nonsaturated scaling reported for joint pretraining.
rows.note: The authors describe the neural-only curve as flat after 25 hours.

rows.subject: NDT3 45M neural-only-pretrained models
rows.stage_stated: pretrained with neural reconstruction objective only
rows.operation_detail: Measured neural reconstruction loss at increasing pretraining-data scales.
rows.value: Neural loss improves with increased pretraining data.
rows.note: The text states that loss improves but does not report a fitted power law or numerical loss values.
rows.check: This is a neural reconstruction loss trend with no power-law fit. It is not an LM loss and gives no form for V5.

source_check.locator_found: Section B.3, paragraph describing Fig. 9A; Fig. 9 caption.

relationships.reason: Aggregate improves with joint data and model scaling, but 45M saturates at 2 khrs. Most pretrained pairs are not significantly different, and authors call the relation to scale noisy (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate R² improved across 31 settings, but the 45M model saturated at 2k hours and most pretrained model pairs did not differ significantly.

reader_labels.reason: The aggregate improves with pretraining scale, and the 350M 2 khr model significantly exceeds other pretrained models except the 350M 200 hr model (R1, R2).

reader_labels.reason: The paper reports gains at every tested downstream-data scale and improved results from jointly scaling data and model size (R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Scaling benefits differ substantially across tasks; some are unclear or minimal, and the largest model degrades on some low-data settings (R4, R5, R7).
